questions.q: Where do the futur simple endings come from?
questions.why: The endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont are the present of avoir (with the -av- of avons/avez dropped), stuck onto the stem.

questions.q: How do you build the future stem of an -re verb like « vendre » ?
choices: Drop the final -e, then add the endings
Use the nous form of the present
questions.why: -er and -ir verbs keep the whole infinitive; -re verbs lose the final -e first, giving vendr- : je vendrai.

questions.q: Conjugate in the futur simple: nous (finir) ___ le travail demain.
questions.why: -ir verbs use the full infinitive as the stem: finir- + -ons. Every future form keeps the r before the ending.

questions.q: Which letter is always present just before a futur simple ending?
questions.why: Every future form contains an r before the ending. That /r/ is what separates « je parlerai » (future) from « je parlais » (imperfect) in speech.

questions.q: Irregular stem: je (être) ___ à Paris l'année prochaine.
questions.why: Être has the stem ser-. The endings never change, so only the stem has to be memorised: je serai, tu seras, il sera.
Aller has the shortest stem in the language, ir-, so the whole future is irai, iras, ira, irons, irez, iront.

questions.q: Which of these future forms is correct for « voir » in the je form?
questions.why: Voir has the stem verr- with a double r. Pouvoir (pourr-), envoyer (enverr-), courir (courr-) and mourir (mourr-) behave the same way.
The e → è shift of the present carries into the future, and unlike the present it applies to all six persons: j'achèterai, nous achèterons.

questions.q: Which verb keeps its é unchanged in the future?
questions.why: Verbs in é are the exception: préférer → je préférerai. Acheter takes è, while appeler and jeter double the consonant (j'appellerai, je jetterai).

questions.q: Complete: Quand j'___ (avoir) le temps, je t'appellerai.
questions.why: After quand, lorsque, dès que and tant que, French uses the future where English uses the present. Avoir's stem is aur-.

questions.q: Build the sentence: As soon as he arrives, we'll eat.
questions.why: Both halves are in the future after dès que — the English present ("as soon as he arrives") does not transfer.
The event is immediate, so the futur proche (aller + infinitive) is the only natural choice. The futur simple suits distant or general statements.
Pleuvoir has the future stem pleuvr- and exists only in the il form: il pleuvra.

questions.q: Say this out loud, making the double r audible.
questions.why: The doubled r of courrai is longer than a single one, and it is the only thing distinguishing « je courais » (imperfect) from « je courrai » (future).

questions.q: Explain what the futur antérieur is, how it is formed, and give one example sentence.
a: Avoir or être in the futur simple + past participle, meaning 'will have done'. Auxiliary choice and participle agreement follow the passé composé rules. Example: J'aurai fini avant midi. / Quand tu arriveras, je serai déjà parti.
questions.why: Once you know the future of avoir and être, the future perfect costs nothing extra: it is just the passé composé with a future auxiliary.
